claim: The possibility of one substitution helps distinguish modifiers from complements.
evidence_summary: Payne and colleagues document one with an inherent-part of-dependent, a relation CGEL treats as complementary.
finding: Reduce the weight of this diagnostic. CGEL already limits it, especially with deverbal nouns.
inference: Does substitution by anaphoric one exclude an of-complement?

evidence.source: John Payne, Geoffrey K. Pullum, Barbara C. Scholz & Eva Berlage (2013). Anaphoric one and its implications. Language 89(4), 794–829.
evidence.passage: §14.1, p. 441. The possibility of one substitution helps distinguish modifiers from complements.
evidence.example: The antecedent is eyes and the anaphoric construction is ones of the team manager. The of-phrase expresses the inherent-part relation.
evidence.establishes: An overt dependent can accompany one in a relation CGEL treats as complementary. The diagnostic retains its previously acknowledged limits.
